items.title: 1.2 Predicting a Quadratic Function from its Graph

source_refs.note: Book p. 3-4: 1.2 factor form from x-intercepts and a third point, Example 3 (Figure 1.5) and Example 4

blocks.text: A quadratic function \(f(x) = ax^{2} + bx + c\) can be determined from its graph by using the factor form if the x-intercepts and one additional point on the curve are known.
If the graph crosses the x-axis at \(x = h\) and \(x = k\), then the function can be written as:

blocks.text_alt: f of x equals a times (x minus h) times (x minus k)

blocks.text: Here, \(a\) is a constant that determines the shape and direction of the parabola. To find \(a\), substitute the coordinates of a third known point into the equation.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
This is 1.1 in reverse. In 1.1 we had the function and found the intercepts; now we have the intercepts and want the function.
Why is a third point needed? The intercepts only give the factors. \(y = (x - 1)(x - 2)\), \(y = 5(x - 1)(x - 2)\) and \(y = -3(x - 1)(x - 2)\) all cut the x-axis at 1 and 2; they differ only in \(a\) (how steep the curve is, and whether it opens up or down). One more point on the curve picks out the single correct \(a\).
If the graph only touches the x-axis at \(x = h\), the factor is repeated: use \(y = a(x - h)^{2}\) (Case-II of 1.1), and again one more point gives \(a\).

blocks.alt: Grid graph of a downward parabola cutting the x-axis at (minus 1, 0) and (1, 0) and reaching its highest point (0, 4) on the y-axis. The curve is y = minus 4x squared plus 4.
blocks.caption: Figure 1.5: the graph given in Example 3 (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Example 3
blocks.problem: Find the function whose graph is shown in Figure 1.5.
steps:
Given: the graph in Figure 1.5 cuts the x-axis at \((-1, 0)\) and \((1, 0)\) and passes through \((0, 4)\).
To find: the quadratic function of the graph.
Method: factor form \(f(x) = a(x - h)(x - k)\). The two x-intercepts give \(h\) and \(k\); the third point gives \(a\).

Step 1: write the factor form
From the figure, \(h = -1\) and \(k = 1\).
\[y = a(x - (-1))(x - 1)\]
\[y = a(x + 1)(x - 1) \quad \text{...(1)}\]
Why: each x-intercept \(x = h\) gives a factor \((x - h)\); for \(h = -1\) this is \((x + 1)\).

Step 2: find \(a\) from \((0, 4)\)
\[4 = a(0 + 1)(0 - 1)\]
\[4 = -a\]
\[a = -4\]
Why: \((0, 4)\) lies on the curve, so its coordinates satisfy (1). The intercepts alone cannot fix \(a\): every \(a(x+1)(x-1)\) has the same intercepts.

Step 3: substitute and simplify
\[y = -4(x + 1)(x - 1)\]
\[= -4(x^{2} - 1)\]
\[y = -4x^{2} + 4\]
Why: \((x + 1)(x - 1) = x^{2} - 1\) (difference of squares).

Check:
\[y(-1) = -4(1) + 4 = 0 \;\checkmark\]
\[y(1) = -4(1) + 4 = 0 \;\checkmark\]
\[y(0) = 4 \;\checkmark\]
Also \(a = -4 < 0\): the graph opens downward, as in the figure.

blocks.title: Example 4
blocks.problem: Find an equation of the graph whose x-intercepts are \(x = 1\) and \(x = 2\) and passes through the point \((3, 4)\).
steps:
Given: x-intercepts \(x = 1\), \(x = 2\); the point \((3, 4)\) lies on the graph.
To find: the equation of the (quadratic) graph.
Method: factor form \(y = a(x - h)(x - k)\) with \(h = 1\), \(k = 2\); then use \((3, 4)\) to find \(a\).

Step 1: factor form
\[y = a(x - 1)(x - 2) \quad \text{...(1)}\]
Why: x-intercepts 1 and 2 give the factors \((x - 1)\) and \((x - 2)\).

Step 2: find \(a\) from \((3, 4)\)
\[4 = a(3 - 1)(3 - 2) = 2a\]
\[a = \dfrac{4}{2} = 2\]
Why: the point lies on the graph, so \(x = 3\), \(y = 4\) satisfy (1).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Intercepts \(x = h\), \(x = k\) give \(y = a(x - h)(x - k)\).
2. A graph touching the x-axis at \(x = h\) gives \(y = a(x - h)^{2}\).
3. Substitute one more point \((x_{1}, y_{1})\) of the graph to find \(a\).
4. The sign of \(a\) must match the picture: \(a > 0\) opens upward, \(a < 0\) downward.
5. Check the answer at all the given points.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Writing the factor for \(x = -1\) as \((x - 1)\). It is \((x - (-1)) = (x + 1)\).
2. Forgetting \(a\) and writing just \(y = (x - h)(x - k)\).
3. Substituting an x-intercept to find \(a\): it gives \(0 = 0\) and no information. Use a point not on the x-axis.
4. Sign slips when solving for \(a\), e.g. \(4 = -a\) gives \(a = -4\), not \(4\).
